item.title: Google Will Soon Share Android Developers' Addresses Publicly
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
"Starting on March 1, 2027, Google will display Android developers' phone numbers and addresses with their apps," reports Engadget, "and users everywhere will be able to see them."
As The Elec has reported, this decision has been met with criticism, specifically from smaller developers who operate out of their homes... [Google] says they have to classify themselves as a trader if they intend to earn money from their apps in any way on a regular basis, and if they already have a consistent frequency of transactions... Once they classify themselves as a trader, they'll have to submit their business identity, phone number and address, which Google will display to users everywhere...
If they fail to comply with these requirements, Google could block their updates from rolling out. Ultimately, the company could remove their apps from the Play store, not just in Europe, but in all regions around the world. The Verge notes that Google doesn't accept PO Boxes for an address like Apple does, forcing people to think of ways to protect their identifying information while still earning money from their apps.
Google said it takes privacy seriously, but with a spokesperson telling Engadget that in addition "we comply with applicable laws" and that Google recognizes "how important it is for users to have accessible support for the apps they install.
"Based on what we have heard from the developer community, we are exploring ways to minimize the developer information displayed publicly while making sure users can still easily reach developers for support."

item.title: Moving Proof-of-Assay’s Explanation Layer to Nosana With Ollama and Qwen2.5
item.author: Cubiczan
item.content:encoded: I got an email from the hackathon team this week: Proof-of-Assay had been shortlisted for the Decentralized Compute track in Round 2 of HackerNoon's Decentralize AI Hackathon, and there was a $70 credit to put an open model on their network. I claimed it on the same account I'd used for an earlier Nosana run. This is what I did with it, including the part that didn't work at first.I'm Shyam, a CFO who works in junior mining finance. Proof-of-Assay is a small audit agent for a problem I actually have: reconciling assay certificates with supplier invoices, lot by lot, and leaving a receipt that someone else can re-verify later.The verdicts are decided by plain Python rules, not by a language model. Expected amount is tonnes times the contracted price. Grade, quantity, and amount mismatches get flagged and priced as cash at risk. Every decision goes into a SHA-256 hash chain. Anyone can run two commands on a laptop and get the same 11-entry chain, ending at 907c7041a4a27a44941acf90699a019c8cfe08b0eb4d3f7ef9c3636c8c6cd5ac:python scripts/reproduce.py python scripts/verify_chain.py # PASS The model has one job: write a short explanation of a verdict the rules already made. I learned why that split matters in October, when I asked a 1.5B Qwen model on Nosana whether a low assay was CLEAN or an EXCEPTION, and it said CLEAN with complete confidence. It was wrong. So this time I didn't ask the model to audit anything. I asked it to explain work the rules had already finished.Synthetic-data disclosure: The eight mining lots in this post are fictional demo fixtures. Amounts are deterministic fixture arithmetic, not real mine payables. Proof-of-Assay is a prototype, not a production auditor.Why move the explanation step at all?Because I don't want that layer to depend on a single AI vendor's API. If the narration is an open-weight model I can start on a rented GPU, I can move it, pin the image, and keep the deterministic core exactly as it is. The audit still runs when the GPU is off; you just don't get the paragraphs. For this hackathon, Nosana was the natural place to host that model, and HackerNoon asked for a progress post. This is that post.The job, the market, and the timeout I didn't getThe setup is a single container. The image is docker.io/ollama/ollama:0.32.6, pinned, serving — Ollama's default 4-bit instruct build, 4.68 GB on disk, 7.6 billion parameters, . The API is OpenAI-compatible at , which is what calls when is set. If that environment variable is missing, the audit still produces the same chain and the narratives are skipped.I wanted a cheaper card first. On November 11, 2026, the NVIDIA 4070 premium market was about $0.10 an hour, and the 3090 premium market — the same one I used in October — was $0.19. I planned a Simple deployment, one replica, with a short container timeout, and I was ready to stop it as soon as the demo was done. The 4070 hosts were all busy, so I took an RTX 3090 at $0.19 an hour. The dashboard's create page also no longer offered the 60-minute auto-stop I had wanted, so the job was set to run to completion with a six-hour cap — about $1.14 if I let it sit. After the $70 shortlist credit, the account had $209.83 to work with. I didn't add a card, and I didn't connect a wallet.The current job definition is in the repo at nosana/proof-of-assay-llm.json.The preload missed, and the docs already had the fixThe first job definition used a entry of type to preload . The container came up healthy. returned 200. The model list was empty.That tracks with the docs, once I went back and looked. Official Nosana resource types are S3 and Hugging Face, not a first-class preload. The documented way to stand up an Ollama endpoint is the obvious one: start the server, then pull the model.On the live deployment, I pulled it by hand with . The job definition in the repo now follows that pattern, and it waits until succeeds instead of sleeping for a fixed five seconds:"entrypoint": ["/bin/sh"], "cmd": [ "-c", "ollama serve & pid=$!; i=0; until ollama list >/dev/null 2>&1 || [ \"$i\" -ge 60 ]; do i=$((i+1)); sleep 1; done; ollama pull \"$MODEL\"; wait $pid" ], "env": { "MODEL": "qwen2.5:7b" } If I start this job again, I shouldn't need the manual pull. I didn't redeploy this run just to prove it — the 3090 was already serving the model, and I didn't want to pay for another startup.The numbers from the live runOnce the model was on the card, I pointed the audit at it and ran the same script anyone can run:export NOSANA_LLM_BASE_URL="https://<deployment-host>" export NOSANA_LLM_MODEL="qwen2.5:7b" python scripts/reproduce.py --explain lots=8 clean=5 exceptions=3 cash_at_risk_usd=289849.19 chain_entries=11 head=907c7041a4a27a44941acf90699a019c8cfe08b0eb4d3f7ef9c3636c8c6cd5ac narration=complete explained=8 failed=0 python scripts/verify_chain.py printed chain_length=11 verification=PASS. The chain head is the same value the fixtures produce with no model in the loop. Narratives are written onto the results for display. They are not hashed into the receipt.I also timed the eight explanation calls separately, using the same prompts the client sends, at 1:43 PM Eastern on November 11, 2026. A first request, made after the model had been pulled but wasn't in VRAM, took 4.010 seconds to return a three-token reply. The eight lot explanations then finished in 10.975 seconds of wall time — 1.371 seconds each on average, ranging from 1.231 to 1.505 seconds. Together they used 1,877 prompt tokens and 712 completion tokens, 2,589 in total. These are measurements from one afternoon on one 3090, not a benchmark.What the model actually wroteThe explanations are plain, and they stay on the numbers they were given. On LOT-003, the grade mismatch, Qwen wrote:The audit identified an exception for Lot ID LOT-003 due to a significant variance in the invoiced amount of $893,174.00 compared to the expected amount of $760,693.50, resulting in a cash at risk of $132,480.50. Additionally, there was a grade mismatch between the invoice grade of 2.85 g/t and the assay grade of 2.41 g/t, further complicating the discrepancy.On LOT-006, the quantity mismatch:The audit identified an exception for LOT-006 due to a variance of $98,215.44 between the invoiced amount ($604,903.44) and the expected amount ($506,688.00). Additionally, there is a quantity mismatch with 1126 tonnes invoiced versus the contracted 960 tonnes. These discrepancies are causing the status to be marked as "EXCEPTION."On LOT-007, the price variance:The audit identified an exception for Lot ID LOT-007, where the invoiced amount of $374,897.25 does not match the expected amount of $315,744.00, resulting in a variance of $59,153.25. This discrepancy is reflected in the high cash at risk of $59,153.25 and has been flagged as an exception due to the significant difference between the expected and invoiced amounts.That's useful for a reviewer. It is also still a paraphrase of rules that already ran. I would not replace with any of those paragraphs, and I'm not going to claim the 7B model is a better auditor than the 1.5B model I asked to decide a verdict in October. It's doing a different job: narrating a decision it was not allowed to make.I'll leave this deployment up long enough for a short demo video and this post, then stop it so the credits don't keep ticking at $0.19 an hour. The job-definition fix is in the public repo, so the next start should pull on its own. I want to keep this pattern — an open model I host, and a core that doesn't care whether the model is there — for later work that needs a short explanation layer. I am not putting the model on the verdict path.The code, the job definition, a static verifier, and the demo video are public:This is a prototype. The lots are fictional. The useful result is that I could move the explanation step onto a decentralized GPU without moving the receipt.

item.title: GTA VI: Console Shortages, Performance Showdowns, $1B More Sales, and Some Tech Issues
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Grand Theft Auto VI "has caused a worldwide shortage of gaming consoles," reports the Washington Post, with the game only playable on the most recent generation of Microsoft's Xbox (Series X or S) or on PlayStation 5: In the United States, Sony's higher-end PlayStation 5 Pro was intermittently sold out even before the release, with major retailers out of stock at its $900 retail price and resellers asking as much as $1,900. In Germany, stores such as MediaMarkt and Saturn are sold out of PS5 models and lower-end Xbox ones... Consoles at Sony-recommended prices are similarly hard to find in other European countries, with third-party resellers offering the device at nearly double the price. In Japan, Sony has gone as far as restricting who is allowed to buy the console to block scalpers. The Sony Store sells it only through a lottery open to buyers with a Japanese account and at least 60 hours of verified PS4 or PS5 playtime. Windows Central notes Xbox One consoles can also stream GTA 6 from Xbox Cloud Gaming. And they argue that Sony's "Plays best on PS5" tagline for GTA 6 "is a lie, it turns out," citing a comparison from the hardware-reviewing YouTube channel Digital Foundry (which has 1.54 million subscribers):
Digital Foundry's analysis seems to suggest in no uncertain terms that the Xbox Series X version is generally superior to the PS5. Digital Foundry says that the PS5 version suffers from frame rate issues far more frequently than the Xbox Series X... The Xbox Series X version supports VRR, which with a compatible display helps offset frame drops and smooth out performance perception. GTA 6's sandbox is among the most complex in history, so it's an impressive feat that it runs as well as it does in general on both PS5 and Xbox Series X systems... This is without Xbox Series X leveraging FSR 4.1 either, which in theory, could push the visuals on Xbox Series X beyond even that of the extremely expensive PS5 Pro. In the end they also acknowledge that "the differences are negligible in reality." But the site TechPowerUp notes recent estimates by Alinea Analytics that PlayStation 5 accounts for 75.7% share of GTA VI sales, or 40 million sales, vs. just 13 million units on Xbox. That's 53 million sales total, representing "an estimated total revenue figure of $4.7 billion... "[P]layer statistics show that around 250,000 players have already spent over 100 hours in-game in its first week."
Meanwhile, The Times of India reports both PS5 and Xbox owners are experiencing console issues that may be related to overheating:
A Polish console repair technician says his workshop has seen a sharp rise in faulty Xbox consoles since GTA 6 came out earlier this month. Xbox is far less common than PlayStation in Poland. Even so, it now accounts for around two of every 10 consoles the shop receives each day. Before GTA 6 came out, it took in roughly 10 Xbox units a month.Owners report overheating, shutdowns mid-session, boot failures and slowdowns. Some machines refuse to install updates or freeze after one. One Series X ran other titles fine but stopped booting after a few days of GTA 6. It now powers on with no video output, then the fan stops and the machine shuts itself off. No common cause has been found yet. Overheating is the main suspect, but Xbox diagnostic tools are limited, so the shop is building its own to read error codes.
PS5 owners ran into trouble first. One unit that kept switching off mid-session logged 40 Main SoC Access Errors, plus seven APU VRM Power Fail and seven SSD Controller Watchdog errors. The technician says liquid metal shifting between the chip and heatsink, a known weak spot on older PS5 models, is often to blame...
A Twitch streamer's PS5 died mid-broadcast while he was riding an ATV through Leonida. The screen froze, artifacts appeared, and the system never booted again, even though there was little dust inside. Reddit posts tell similar stories. One Series X owner says the console would not power on the morning after a long session, and a dead power supply is suspected. Another managed about 10 minutes of play before a local repair shop blamed the motherboard...
Neither Microsoft nor Sony has confirmed that GTA 6 is behind the failures.
In related news, the social media team at Microsoft-owned GitHub "published and subsequently deleted a bizarrely brazen post on X," reports Kotaku. The tweet pointed to the 58,000 stars earned by a new project launched in August — the PlayStation5 emulator AnyPS5, which it said can be used for "rewriting PS5 executables to run on Windows and Linux. Does changing where games run cross a legal line?" [T]he video that was contained within GitHub's post highlighted that users' efforts to improve the AnyPS5 emulator were primarily driven by the release of GTA 6.
The article notes GTA VI's publisher Take Two has been "actively shooting down all of the GitHub repositories attempting to vibe-code a PC port of GTA 6 over the past week."

item.title: Will AI Bots Ever Catch on for Online Shopping?
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
"If you currently use an AI agent that signs in to your account with your credentials, it may no longer be able to connect," American Express told its customers today (according to Slashdot reader Smonster). And ahile Walmart's site welcomes AI agents, there's blocks or limitations on them from Amazon, eBay, Kohl's and United Airlines, CNBC reports. And other sites "have added provisions to their terms of service spelling out that they're not liable if users' AI-driven purchases go wrong..."
The hiccups threaten to stunt the growth of shopping agents by creating a clunky and frustrating experience for users who are just starting to experiment with the tools. The question of who takes the blame when a transaction goes wrong also remains unclear.
Despite those challenges, analysts remain bullish about agentic commerce's potential. U.S. revenue from agentic commerce could reach up to $1 trillion by 2030, analysts at McKinsey and ICSC forecast in April. Retailers and tech companies are also positioning agents as a helping hand for holiday shopping. Walmart on Tuesday touted its partnership with Meta, saying consumers could "put an AI agent to work" to nab Black Friday deals....
For users hoping to turn their online shopping over to AI agents, the experience can be unpredictable. Agents encounter a patchwork of permissions across various websites. Retailers such as Coach and Gap allow AI bots to browse but not check out, while others such as Target sometimes "block shopping agents by accident," according to an audit conducted in August by agent security company Billions Network. Amazon has responded the most aggressively to agents by walling off its site entirely. The company rankled Elon Musk last month after it prevented his Grok Bot from placing orders. In September, the company also blocked Meta's Muse from shopping on its platform, saying it never agreed to participate in the program. And last November, Amazon sued Perplexity, accusing the startup of concealing its Comet agent, which can purchase products on behalf of users. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said the company expects "over time, to partner with third-party agents," but that any partnerships will require the right "value exchange" between agents and retailers... For now, agents remain a niche tool for shopping, with agentic purchases making up just 0.4% of global e-commerce transactions and 0.2% of value, according to Bain & Co. research published earlier this month... But retailers may not be able to ignore them forever. Roughly a quarter of Muse's 10 million users are shopping online via an AI agent with an average spend of $200 per order, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said in October. The article notes bots often "get stumped by login requirements at checkout. In some cases, the agents may require human intervention to bypass a Captcha test and continue browsing...
"A Visa study published earlier this month instructed 22 models from 12 AI labs to carry out a range of shopping tasks, such as buying a TV, a laptop and a hair appliance. The agents failed about 43% of test runs, and in more than half of those failed runs, an agent purchased a product "that did not meet the customer's identified requirements," according to the study..."

item.title: I Tested Google's ARTEMIS: Can AI Agents Really Automate Android Testing?
item.author: Ishank Choudhary
item.content:encoded: A reel went around this week claiming Google had quietly open-sourced a tool called ARTEMIS that lets Claude Code, Codex or Cursor drive an Android phone. The claims: about 15k GitHub stars, 99% success on 100+ real phone tasks, it opens apps, taps and types, it tests your app after every change and hands back a report with screenshots and logs.My team ships Android apps, and the slowest part of every change is still someone tapping through the same five screens on a device. If an agent in my editor can do that for me, I want it. But I don't trust star counts or success rates from a 30-second video, so I cloned the repo, booted an emulator on a Linux box and ran it.Short version: the project is real, the numbers in the reel are a little off, and it did every job I gave it. The most useful thing I found was a failure mode, not a feature.The repo is github.com/google/artemis, Apache-2.0, written in Python. It was created on 13 August 2026 and had 17,876 stars and 1,989 forks when I checked on 22 November 2026. The README pitches it as "Let AI assistants and test suites use real phones like a human."Under the hood it's a LangGraph agent that reads the screen through Android's accessibility tree (it installs its own small Accessibility Helper APK on the device, with UIAutomator2 as the fallback), looks at screenshots with a vision model, and acts through ADB. You can drive it four ways: a web console, a CLI, a Python SDK, and an MCP server, which is the part the reel was about.It has two execution profiles:: one model in a tight observe-think-act loop. The README says 3 to 5 seconds per step. There's no plan, no pre-action safety check, no verifier and no report.: a multi-agent graph. A Planner writes a Markdown task plan with and items, an Operator executes it, a Safety Net vets each single action before it fires, a Checker audits the result at the end, and an optional Outputter writes a report. The README says 15 to 40 seconds per step.The reel's claims, checkedOpen-sourced on Google's GitHub: confirmed. It's under the org.: low. It was 17,876 when I looked.99% success on 100+ real phone tasks: needs correcting. The README's chart shows 99.1% Pass@1 on AndroidWorld, Google Research's benchmark of 116 tasks across 20 apps. AndroidWorld runs on an emulator, not real phones, and the number is self-reported. The repo doesn't include the harness or the model settings used for that run, so I couldn't reproduce it.Opens apps, taps and types: confirmed in my runs.Works on a plugged-in phone or emulator: emulator confirmed. USB phones are documented, but I didn't test one.Tests your own app after each change: documented. takes an that installs an APK before the run. I didn't test that path.Returns a report with screenshots and logs: partly. Pro can write a report if you ask for one, and the MCP tools return trace summaries, screenshots and Logcat. Flash gives you a trace, not a report.: confirmed. iOS is on the roadmap.: broader than that. It supports Gemini (the default), Claude, GPT-4o, OpenRouter, xAI and local models through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. I only ran Gemini.Works with Claude Code, Codex and Cursor: the installer writes configs for all three, plus Antigravity, Windsurf, VS Code, Cline/Roo and OpenClaw. I didn't run it inside any of them. I talked to the MCP server from my own client, which I explain below.I used a Debian box with 8 vCPUs and 15 GB of RAM, with nested KVM available. existed but my user couldn't open it, so I gave it a temporary ACL and took it away when I was done. With KVM working, a headless Android 14 emulator is straightforward:sdkmanager "platform-tools" "emulator" "system-images;android-34;google_apis;x86_64" echo no | avdmanager create avd -n artemis34 \ -k "system-images;android-34;google_apis;x86_64" -d pixel_6 emulator -avd artemis34 -no-window -no-audio -no-snapshot \ -gpu swiftshader_indirect -memory 3072 -cores 4 & adb shell getprop sys.boot_completed # 1 after ~50 s git clone https://github.com/google/artemis.git && cd artemis uv sync # Python 3.12 venv uv run artemis doctor The official path is , which also installs ADB, scrcpy and FFmpeg and offers to wire up your IDEs. I went the manual route so I could see each piece. came back "Ready (optional gaps)". The Gemini key was detected, the emulator was connected at 1080x2400, and scrcpy was missing, which only turns off video replay.First run: the default model was busyMy first task failed after three minutes with LLM call timed out after 180 seconds. The logs were full of Gemini 503s ("This model is currently experiencing high demand"). The default config points every node at , falling back to , and both were overloaded right then. A separate preset in the same file names , which now returns 404 for new users.The fix is three lines in : "default": { "provider": "google", - "model": "gemini-3.8-flash", + "model": "gemini-3.6-flash", "thinking_level": "medium", "fallback": { "provider": "google", - "model": "gemini-3.7-flash", + "model": "gemini-3.5-flash", Plus the history-chunking model further down. After that, everything ran. If you put this in CI, pin a model you know you have capacity on, and use a fallback from a different model family, not just the next version down.Task 1: the README example, from the CLIuv run artemis run "Open Settings, find Battery and tell me the current battery level" \ --profile flash -s emulator-5554 It finished in 28 seconds, including spawning the background daemon, in three turns: launch Settings, tap the Battery row, report "The current battery level is 100%." adb shell dumpsys battery agreed: level 100. It made 5 model calls.This is the bit that matters for coding agents. The server is a FastMCP app you launch over stdio:uv run artemis mcp --generate-config claude # or codex, cursor, antigravity uv run artemis mcp --install all # writes global config + rules The Claude config it prints is just .venv/bin/python -m mcp_server with set. For Codex it writes a TOML block with startup_timeout_sec = 120.I didn't have Claude Code or Codex on this box, so I wrote a small Python MCP client that launches the server the same way those configs do and calls the tools directly. Same transport, same server, same tool calls. It shows exactly what an editor agent sees:params = StdioServerParameters( command=f"{REPO}/.venv/bin/python", args=["-m", "mcp_server"], cwd=REPO, env=dict(os.environ, PYTHONUNBUFFERED="1", PYTHONPATH=REPO)) async with stdio_client(params) as (r, w), ClientSession(r, w) as s: await s.initialize() res = await s.call_tool("mobile_run_task", { "task_desc": goal, "model": "Flash", "device_serial": "emulator-5554"}) # returns a trace_id at once; then poll: await s.call_tool("mobile_manage_task", {"action": "status", "trace_id": tid}) await s.call_tool("mobile_inspect_trace", {"action": "view_summary", "trace_id": tid}) The server reported itself as and listed five tools:: starts a Flash or Pro run in the background and returns a straight away. It takes , , and .: , , or to steer a run that's going wrong.: a screenshot, or a numbered element list with bounds on a 0â€“1000 grid.: step-by-step reasoning and actions after the fact.: an environment doctor that tells the agent what to fix.Their descriptions and schemas add up to 17,696 characters. That's context your agent loads on every session whether it touches a phone or not, so I'd only enable this server in projects that need it. with came back in 1.6 seconds: 5 of 5 required checks passed, the device probe saw 24 elements, and the hierarchy came from the helper. The hierarchy view is compact and agent-friendly. Here's the Battery screen:[6] Text: 'Battery charging, 100 percent.' | Bounds: [912,0][931,53] [9] Text: '100 %' | Bounds: [58,249][361,342] [13] Text: 'Battery Saver' | Bounds: [58,512][347,542] [14] Text: 'Off' | Bounds: [58,542][105,563] Task 2: dark theme over MCP, FlashGoal: "Open Settings, go to Display and turn on Dark theme, then confirm Dark theme is on."Step 1 (5.4s) click({'target': 8}) # back to main Settings Step 2 (8.4s) swipe({'direction': 'up'}) Step 3 (11.8s) click({'target': 14}) # Display Step 4 (14.5s) click({'target': 20}) # Dark theme toggle Step 5 (17.4s) report_task_status({'status': 'completed', ...}) reported after 20.2 seconds. That's about 3 seconds per step, which matches the README. I didn't trust the agent's word for it: adb shell cmd uimode night said "Night mode: no" before the run and "Night mode: yes" after. It made 9 model calls.It also handled its starting point well. The phone was still on the Battery page from Task 1, so its first move was to go back rather than relaunch Settings.Goal: "Open the Contacts app, create a new contact named Ada Lovelace with mobile number 555-0100, save it, and verify the contact shows up in the contacts list. Report the steps you took."The Planner wrote a three-milestone plan with a item ("contact details saved successfully") and an ("contact 'Ada Lovelace' is visible in the contacts list"). The Operator then launched Contacts, skipped the Google sign-in promo, tapped +, typed Ada, Lovelace and 555-0100 into the right fields, saved, and navigated back to the list. The first seven actions came 6 to 8 seconds apart. The last two took longer because of more 503 retries.The work was real. The contacts provider had the row:display_name=Ada Lovelace, data1=555-0100, mimetype=vnd.android.cursor.item/phone_v2 Then the final review ran. By that point my Gemini key, which was on the free tier, had used up its daily limit of 20 requests for . The Checker's call came back 429, and ARTEMIS logged this:Final check errored (); releasing fail-open. Run outcome: task_status=completed, tests(passed=0, failed=0, inconclusive=2) Automation 'web_..._8286c6ef' is success So the MCP status said , with a of 0 passed and 2 inconclusive. The device state was correct. But if I had wired this into a pipeline that only checked , a run whose verifier never ran would have gone green.That's a design choice, and the data is there: is machine-readable and clearly says . You just have to read it. If you use ARTEMIS as a test gate, fail on anything other than failed == 0 and inconclusive == 0, and run with verification_level="checkpoints" or so the asserts are checked along the way, not just once at the exit.Pro also costs more. This run took 360 seconds and 26 model calls, and ARTEMIS's own usage log shows about 4.5 times the prompt volume of the Flash dark-theme run, for a task with nine actions.The README's leaderboard chart puts ARTEMIS at 99.1% Pass@1 on AndroidWorld's 116 tasks. FinalRun is next at 97.4%, the human baseline is 80.0%, and Gemini 2.5 Computer Use sits at 69.7%. AndroidWorld is a solid benchmark: 116 hand-crafted tasks, instantiated with random parameters on a live emulator, with durable reward signals. But this chart is ARTEMIS's own, the repo doesn't ship the eval harness or say which model and profile produced the number, and AndroidWorld runs on an emulator. "99% on real phones" isn't what it says.What I can say from three tasks: three out of three were done correctly on the device, and I checked each one with adb rather than trusting the agent's report. That's a sanity check, not a benchmark.A physical phone over USB.Claude Code, Codex or Cursor themselves. I used the same stdio MCP server from my own client.Installing and testing my own APK through .Claude, GPT-4o or local models. Gemini only.Video replay (no scrcpy on this box), Logcat capture, and the Pro written report.The pattern ARTEMIS's own rules file pushes is the right one. The coding agent uses ARTEMIS to explore the app and find the real path through the UI, then writes a deterministic test (Espresso, UIAutomator, Maestro, whatever you use) that runs without a model in the loop. item.title: Enterprises Are Scaling AI Faster Than They Can Control It
item.author: Sanford Diday
item.content:encoded: In June, I argued that most enterprise AI investments fail for an infrastructure reason, not a model reason: organizations have no system for capturing, governing, and reusing what their AI tools learn. The missing layer, in my view, is a stateful runtime that remembers, governs, and lets anyone audit it, and this piece tests that claim against six months of new data. The data have not softened that argument. They have sharpened it. Adoption climbed. Governance moved too, but more slowly than adoption, and the European Union pushed back the compliance deadline toward which enterprises were racing. That delay raises the cost of waiting rather than lowering it.The Divide Held. Adoption Surged. Returns Stalled.The original claim came from MIT Project NANDA's : ninety-five percent of enterprise generative AI pilots produced no measurable P&L return, against $30 to $40 billion in enterprise investment (Challapally et al.). McKinsey's newest global survey, which reached 1,719 respondents in ninety-seven countries in May and June 2026, is the closest thing to a one-year check on that number, and it does not describe a turnaround. Thirty-seven percent of respondents now attribute at least some EBIT impact to AI, essentially flat against last year. Only six percent qualify as "AI high performers," attributing five percent or more of EBIT to AI with a self-described significant effect, also flat (Tinkoff et al.). Adoption outran value capture again. Eighty percent say AI has made them personally more productive; fewer than four in ten can point to a dollar figure their organization can defend (Tinkoff et al.). Executives inside large firms report a similar disconnect: in a survey of 1,221 of them, more than four in five say their AI programs are beating expectations, yet only about two in five firms formally require teams to track business impact (Economist Enterprise).What moved was scale, not proof. Forty-four percent of organizations report AI scaling across the enterprise, up from thirty-eight percent a year earlier. Fifty-six percent now use AI in three or more business functions, up from fifty-one percent. Forty percent of large organizations are scaling AI agents in at least one function, up from twenty-seven percent (Tinkoff et al.). More of the enterprise is running more AI through more functions, and last year's return question still lacks a clear answer. That combination, not any single statistic, is the pattern worth naming.Nearly Half of Enterprise AI Runs Outside GovernanceIn June, I described a shadow AI economy without a clean enterprise-wide figure to anchor it. Akamai's 2026 Enterprise AI Usage Risk Report, which draws on data from LayerX after Akamai acquired the company, supplies one and counts what actually matters: the conversation, not the headcount. Across enterprise AI traffic, 47.11 percent of conversations happen through personal identities rather than corporate accounts. Even inside corporate-identity traffic, about 14.4 percent of conversations run on personal AI licenses rather than enterprise ones (Akamai). The split varies sharply by platform. Users reach ChatGPT, consumer Copilot, and DeepSeek mostly through personal accounts, with more than sixty percent of conversations coming from personal identities, while enterprise-focused offerings run overwhelmingly through corporate accounts: 90.55 percent of Microsoft 365 Copilot conversations and 98.15 percent of Gemini Enterprise conversations (Akamai). That uneven split is the finding. Where a company deploys a tool it controls, usage follows it; where it does not, nearly half of all AI conversation volume routes around governance entirely and carries proprietary prompts and outputs through accounts no compliance team can see. Because this is a security vendor's telemetry rather than a survey, it measures what employees do, not what they say they do.The risk concentrates, too. The average enterprise user takes part in thirty-six AI conversations, but the bottom half of users have twelve or fewer while the top five percent have at least 144, and the deepest conversations run to eighteen prompts or more (Akamai). Browser extensions are another channel that security teams scrutinize too little: nearly seventy-five percent of AI extensions request high or critical permissions, and 16.31 percent carry known vulnerabilities, against 10.8 percent of extensions overall (Akamai).Abstract risk became a concrete incident in March. A Meta engineer asked an internal AI agent to analyze a technical question a colleague had posted to an internal forum. The agent posted its own answer back to the forum directly, without asking the engineer first. The advice was bad, and the employee who had asked the question acted on it. The resulting changes gave engineers who lacked authorization access to company and user-related data for two hours. Meta classified the incident Sev 1, its second-highest internal severity tier, according to an incident report The Information reviewed (Silberling). The reporting describes no outside attacker. Meta Superintelligence safety and alignment director Summer Yue described a separate incident in a post on X the month before: her own AI agent deleted her full email inbox despite her instruction that it confirm with her before acting (Silberling).Neither incident was fundamentally a failure of model capability. Both happened where no approval step sat between what an agent decided and what it could do unsupervised. That is the governance infrastructure from my June argument, not a hypothetical: interaction capture, codified knowledge, access controls, audit trails, and enforcement that actually works, rather than five components existing only in a policy document. Meta is not a company short on engineering talent. The failure sat exactly where I located it in June, in the infrastructure between the model and the organization, not in the model. Two incidents are a small sample, but they show the shape of the risk.Protocols Standardized in Thirteen Months; Governance Still LagsAnthropic's Model Context Protocol launched in November 2024. By December 2025, thirteen months later, Anthropic reported more than ninety-seven million monthly SDK downloads across Python and TypeScript, more than 10,000 active public servers, and adoption by ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Visual Studio Code (Anthropic). On December 9, 2025, Anthropic donated MCP to the newly formed Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation that Anthropic, Block, and OpenAI co-founded with support from Google, Microsoft, AWS, Cloudflare, and Bloomberg. That donation is what a maturing standard looks like once its original owner stops needing to own it (Anthropic). The protocol question open in June is closing. The governance question is not.The EU Delayed High-Risk Rules. Waiting Now Costs More.In June, I flagged an eighteen-month window before AI vendor relationships became expensive to unwind and tied it loosely to the EU AI Act's original compliance calendar. That calendar changed. Enforcement of the Act's transparency rules and general-purpose AI obligations began on schedule, August 2, 2026: chatbots must disclose they are automated, content AI generates or alters needs a machine-readable mark, and general-purpose AI providers must document training content and share the information regulators require (Markovic). But the European Union's Digital Omnibus pushed the Act's high-risk system obligations, which cover tools like recruitment screening and credit scoring, from August 2026 to December 2, 2027 (European Parliament and Council, Digital Omnibus). Penalties stayed tiered rather than shrinking: prohibited practices still carry fines up to thirty-five million euros or seven percent of global turnover, while high-risk and transparency violations carry up to fifteen million euros or three percent, whichever is higher (European Parliament and Council, AI Act, art. 99). Correction: the thirty-five million euro tier applies to prohibited practices, not high-risk violations, which sit in the lower tier.A later deadline is not a reason to slow down. An organization spending the next twelve months building the governance stack will finish with weeks to spare before December 2027, and with a long head start on whoever waits for the deadline to start caring. A later deadline bought the organizations already behind more time to remain behind when it arrives.Adoption Outruns Governance. Failures Cost Millions.Deloitte published its 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise report in January, drawing on 3,235 business and IT leaders across twenty-four countries whom it surveyed between August and September 2025. In Deloitte's fall 2025 survey, twenty-one percent said they had a mature governance model for agentic AI specifically, against seventy-four percent who expected to use AI agents at least moderately within two years (Deloitte AI Institute). ISACA's research shows a similar climb: twenty-eight percent of organizations reported a formal, comprehensive AI policy in 2025; thirty-eight percent report one now (ISACA). Neither number shows anyone has solved the problem, though ISACA's does show real, year-over-year progress worth stating outright. Adoption still runs ahead of both: fifty-six percent of organizations now use AI in three or more business functions (Tinkoff et al.), against governance rates between twenty-one and thirty-eight percent. The surveys measure different things, so the margin shifts with the survey, and the comparison is directional, not exact.Governance is thinnest after launch. A 2026 survey of large firms already using advanced AI found about three in five review AI systems during development and before deployment, but fewer than two in five continue that oversight once a system is live, and one in eight reviews only when something goes wrong. About three in five leading adopters have autonomous systems doing real work, yet fewer than half mandate a formal framework for them. The firms furthest ahead invested in the control layer before they invested in autonomy (Economist Enterprise). Cost reinforces the point: just over half of firms with unified data architectures, and roughly two-thirds of those with less integrated environments, name data storage, movement, and duplication as their biggest ongoing AI expense, more than double the share pointing to computing infrastructure (Economist Enterprise).The price of skipping that control layer is measurable. In EY's 2025 survey of 975 C-suite leaders at firms with more than $1 billion in revenue, ninety-nine percent reported financial losses from AI-related risks, sixty-four percent lost more than $1 million, and the average loss was $4.4 million; those that had defined clear responsible-AI principles reported thirty percent fewer risks (Depa). Leaders may not know which controls to apply: when EY asked respondents to match appropriate controls to five AI-related risks, only twelve percent of C-suite respondents answered all five correctly (Depa). Separately, firms with safeguards such as real-time monitoring had about a third fewer failures, a different measure from the risk count above (Economist Enterprise).Gartner's forecast puts a number on what happens to deployments without those safeguards: by the end of 2027, organizations will cancel more than forty percent of agentic AI projects now underway because of escalating costs, unclear business value, or inadequate risk controls (Gartner). None of those causes is model capability. My reading is that the forty percent are the deployments teams launched without the control layer this piece keeps describing, the ones that do not survive contact with an audit, an incident, or a board that finally asks who approved it.The Core Claim Held: Build Infrastructure Before ScaleNone of the six months since June required revising the core claim. The organizations pulling ahead are still the ones treating AI governance as infrastructure to build before scale, not paperwork to produce after an incident. MCP confirmed that quickly: it went from launch to industry standard in about thirteen months because enough of the ecosystem decided interoperability was worth building deliberately, together, rather than patching case by case. Governance infrastructure inside individual enterprises is moving in the same direction, just earlier and more slowly. The comparison is loose, since analysts measure MCP growth in downloads and governance progress in survey percentages, but ISACA's climb from twenty-eight percent to thirty-eight percent in one year looks like the early stretch of an adoption curve. MIT Sloan professor Eric So adds a human-side cost: overreliance on AI puts tacit institutional knowledge at risk, especially among younger workers (Stackpole).Organizations that treat the new 2027 deadline as a pause button will spend the next twelve months exactly where they are now. The ones that treat it as the time they were already going to need will spend it closing the distance between what their AI systems do and what anyone can prove they may do. That is the bet I laid out at the start: the layer enterprises are missing is not a smarter model, but a stateful runtime that remembers, governs, and lets anyone audit it. Disney's Chas Murphy gives the practitioner's version: the differentiator, he says, will not be "the next model that's the game changer" but "how professionally they build out their guardrails and their evaluators" (Economist Enterprise). Six months of new data have not changed my mind about which bet wins the decade.European Parliament and Council of the European Union. item.title: Chinese Data Center Tied to Alice Huang Found Using Nvidia's Powerful AI Chips
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Friday Nvidia's stock showed a 30.95% drop over the last month, and a 37% drop from its October 2nd high of $239.24. But it managed a 4.83% gain for the week — after some bad news hit Friday morning...
A Chinese data center with ties to Alice Huang (the suspected Chinese spy-agency asset) "has installed hardware with Nvidia's powerful Blackwell AI chips," writes Gizmodo, citing a Friday morning report from Bloomberg. Those chips are "among Nvidia's most powerful products," writes Bloomberg, and their presence was confirmed by "a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November," (offering the hardware as collateral for a $14 million loan, according to bank filings seen by Bloomberg News). A second Chinese company (this one controlled by a Tokyo-based parent company) also described a server with Nvidia's advanced Blackwell chips in documents for a similar loan in late 2025 from, Bloomberg reports:
The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia's Blackwell processors found their way into a Chinese data center that has ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. [Alice Huang has ties to "a number of companies" that invested in the second company, and its president is her husband Kang Wei.]
These processors were until recently Nvidia's most powerful data center products, and they've always been illegal to ship to China without a US license. President Donald Trump has explicitly said he doesn't want these chips — which OpenAI and Anthropic PBC use to train their most cutting-edge models — going to the Asian country, at least for now. Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, meanwhile, once claimed they were too big to smuggle: a standard two-meter-tall GB300 NVL72 server rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, can weigh more than 1,500 kilograms (3,300 pounds) and is about the size of a gigantic fridge...
Shanghai Shuoyao — the company that procured the GB300 rack and offered it as collateral — is active at the data center linked to Alice Huang and also has significant overlap with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is under US investigation over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia chips to China, Bloomberg has reported. Shanghai Shuoyao, which hasn't responded to Bloomberg queries over the past year, confirmed this month in a rare public statement that it is one of Megaspeed's service providers, describing the partnership as "limited to ordinary commercial cooperation."
Megaspeed, meanwhile, used a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project in 2024 to describe its largest data center to investors, dubbing the site a "specific area" facility in an unnamed country... The parameters they've outlined in construction plans reviewed by Bloomberg — specifically, the total processing power as compared to the energy input — would be extremely difficult to satisfy with chips from Chinese companies such as Huawei Technologies Co.
Bloomberg says Nvidia "has not answered repeated queries," though they add that Nvida "for years insisted that there was no black market for its products."
The article also notes that Megaspeed (where Alice Huang worked) "won a coveted stamp of approval from Nvidia within four days of its creation" in 2023, and went on to become Nvidia's largest customer in Southeast Asia.

item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Firefox 161 (released Tuesday) promises "A better Firefox, thanks to you. All of these improvements began with a community request." In a Thanksgiving-themed message, they wrote "Here's to the passionate people who keep us moving forward."
Choose which sites always open with VPN. Our free built-in VPN just got one of its most requested upgrades. Pick sites where the VPN always turns on, and sites where it stays off because they work better without it. Bonus: VPN data is unlimited through January. Use it as much as you like until then... Set your own shortcuts . Create keyboard shortcuts for what you use most, like opening tabs, saving pages or closing windows. Type "about:keyboard" in the address bar.
See images appear as they load. Firefox now supports JPEG XL, an image format that lets you see a preview of the full image before it downloads.
Neowin notes Firefox is also committing to its redesign:
Mozilla has been trying to win over users from Chromium-based browsers, hoping they pick up Firefox. To do so, aside from still supporting uBlock Origin, the firm made a big design shift this year by introducing Nova, so that users on the other side can feel they are familiar with it, as it brings the more common, modern rounded corner design philosophy, which Google's Chrome has been using for quite a while... However, as is usually the case, not everyone has been on-board with Nova and they are completely fine to feel that way; Mozilla also understands this which is why it offered a way to opt-out of it by tweaking a configuration setting via about:config. However, this week the firm announced that it is going to take that option away.
In a post on its official Mozilla Connect forum, which was shared with us by Neowin forum member ecmram, the Firefox team confirmed that it will remove the config toggle preference for reverting to the old design next month in December. The company says that the rollout of Nova is now complete, and it wants to lock the preference to ensure that Firefox performs as intended and to prevent unexpected browser behavior. As such, anyone who has previously used the browser.nova.enabled preference to disable the redesign will automatically get Nova starting next month, thus wiping the official way to return to the previous UI once the change takes effect.
On the positive side, Mozilla is not entirely ignoring feedback from users who are unhappy with the redesign. The company says it has introduced several changes based on community feedback, including a new set of Classic Themes with the latest version 161, that offer flat colors without gradients. These can be found under about:addons, and one of them even mimics the older Proton design with a gray appearance. There is a new Fire toolbar button too that clears history with a single-click.

item.title: Vendor Lock-In Is Creating a Market for Escape
item.author: Chris Gale
item.content:encoded: Jeff Bezos famously said, “Your margin is my opportunity.” Where incumbents carried generous margins and sought rents, a hungry challenger saw room to win by serving customers better and charging less. Today, the line could be, “Your switching costs are my opportunity.” A new wave of enterprises is building a business out of jailbreaking customers from platforms.And “platform” used to be a positive word. Investors liked platforms. Customers liked them too. And the latter dependably picked a platform over an agglomeration of best-in-class solutions. Our own little outfit is no exception. Maybe you weren’t excited about the platform over the best in class alternative. But the platform application fit with every other platform application better, and the combined cost and security were and remain seductive.Well, the security may remain seductive. But the pricing is changing.We have lived this at our own firm. ActiveCampaign notified us that our monthly plan would move from $295.29 to $399.46 on December 19th, an increase of about 35%, with the new rate applying unless we completed cancellation before that date. ActiveCampaign's price increases stem from a multi-year shift from simple email marketing to an all-in-one, AI-powered automation platform.But putting that aside, its last raise was in 2021, the peak of the zero-interest-rate tech bubble. Venture capital and growth-equity funds like those that put their then-cheap money into the company typically look for an exit within five to seven years. So it’s time to monetize the switching costs developed over that period. Essentially firms like ours whose contacts and CRM intelligence are in the platform. But to the extent that money is being put into improving the platform, it’s not easy to see.The market is also saturated, and smaller firms like ours require proportionately more handing than large enterprises for less revenue, so we’re no longer welcome unless we’re willing to pay closer to what big companies are seeking to pay. We’re not going to get better service out of this price increase, but large enterprises might.Anyone who has read about the history of redlining in the U.S. and how places like Harlem paid for America’s suburbs will start to get aspects of the picture, though in an exponentially more insidious and morally corrupt form. Not to pick on ActiveCampaign, because despite their attempting to mollify us by inviting us to pay a little bit less in absolute terms by paying it all in advance, they’ve been accommodating enough about letting us get off here, and us letting them try to focus on the large enterprises.With Cision - our reporter database and wire service platform - we had stayed through earlier price increases even though the service wasn’t delivering anything new or better that we wanted. We did this because we assumed that in exchange for our loyalty they would help us out if we needed it.As we’ve pursued a pivot, we asked for help with the cost. They couldn’t give us any, and we gave notice of non-renewal. We then learned that services couldn’t be removed mid-contract and they were bent on holding us down. While previously it was just the reporter database we wanted to address, now we’ve realized that while we saw them as a partner who would reward loyalty, the company is actually a risk and can amplify and compound problems if and when they occur. So we are now moving off both of their services. We’re also looking more carefully at the ownership structure and financing of the tech solutions and platforms we use, because we don’t want our data and workflows in the hands of an outfit that must monetize its switching costs on that same five-to-seven-year clock.Neither vendor lost us over a feature or poor service. The products were great, exactly what we needed. Though interestingly in both cases once we left the platform we realized we had been missing superior services from competitors or we could just build what we needed internally. It wasn’t a priority to find alternatives, but both companies made it one for us, and we have benefited, as have our own clients.This is the problem with switching costs as a competitive advantage.The more a company raises prices, no matter how much it claims the increases fund improvements the customer doesn’t recall asking for, the more the switching costs become a bitter experience. As one operations leader said within earshot of me recently, “I hate platforms, I don’t want us to be on a platform.” And as the cheap money becomes scarce, and U.S. policymaking does that it has been doing in very recent years, that sentiment is likely to increase.Vertice, a software-procurement firm that tracks what its customers pay, reports preliminary SaaS inflation of 14.3 percent in September 2026, after a record 16.4% in June. Over the same twelve months, US consumer prices rose 3.7 percent according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI release of October 14th. Vertice’s figure is a vendor-published average drawn from its own customer base, not an official statistic. But Microsoft’s own pricing announcement shows the pattern at the largest platform, effective July 1st Microsoft 365 Business Basic rose from $6 to $7 per user per month. That’s 16 percent. Business Standard went from $12.50 to $14 So 12 percent. And Microsoft 365 E3 has gone from $36 to $39 for 8 percent. Existing customers move to the new prices at renewal.But it’s also the tech talent marketWhen a software company loses confidence that it can win customers by building better products, it stops trying to keep customers because they love the product. It tries to keep them because they can’t leave.Challenger, Gray & Christmas counted 171,501 announced US technology job cuts through October 2026. That is up 21 percent from a year earlier and already more than the 154,445 for all of 2025. Layoffs.fyi lists about 149,000 tech employees laid off at 366 companies worldwide so far this year. Companies increasingly say AI is the reason. The evidence for that is thin.Challenger has tracked AI as the most-cited reason for layoffs for several months running in 2026, but laid-off workers describe something else. In a February 2026 Gallup survey of more than 23,000 US workers, only about 1 percent of those laid off said AI directly caused their job loss. Most cited restructuring, cost-cutting and economic conditions, and that includes a shift away from customer-centrism to rent-raising. A study reported by Fortune in August 2026 foud some of the companies studied cut staff before investing much in AI, allegedly to free up money for it. Revelio Labs found that companies announcing AI-driven layoffs had actually been adding AI talent more slowly than their industry peers, at a median of about 11 percent over two years compared with more than 13 percent. Forrester estimates that only 6 percent of US jobs will be automated by 2030. If AI were doing the work of the people being let go, these numbers would look different.The layoffs line up better with a change in where companies want their people. Support and product engineering are shrinking. Sales, account management and migration programs are protected or growing. And prices are rising on customers who find it hard to leave.Start with Broadcom and VMware. VMware had more than 38,000 employees at the start of 2023 and about 16,000 two years later, according to Business Insider. Smaller customers lost direct support and were routed to a distributor, with response times stretching to a week or more. European cloud providers documented price increases of 800 percent to 1,500 percent. Even so, a January 2026 CloudBolt survey of 302 IT decision-makers found that only 4 percent had fully replaced VMware. Untangling the dependencies typically takes 18 to 24 months. The study concluded that Broadcom is deliberately accepting customer churn while maximizing margins on the customers who remain. Support quality was a top concern for 78 percent of respondents, and 85 percent expect further price increases. None of this depends on AI.Broadcom ran the same playbook after buying CA Technologies in 2018, and Constellation Research analyst Ray Wang said when the VMware layoffs began that this is how Broadcom makes money from its acquisitions.At Salesforce, CEO Marc Benioff claimed in September 2025 that AI agents had allowed the company to cut its customer support workforce from about 9,000 to 5,000. He says he has held engineering headcount flat at roughly 15,000 for two years. In January 2026 he said the company was hiring 20 percent more account executives. In August 2025, Salesforce raised prices on Enterprise and Unlimited editions of Sales Cloud, Service Cloud and other products by an average of 6 percent, after a 9 percent increase in 2023. AI is harder to accept as the explanation, given that Business Insider reported Agentforce usage remained relatively low and the product hadn’t matched the company’s demos. In early 2026, Salesforce cut roles on the Agentforce team itself.In May 2026 Cloudflare eliminated more than 1,100 positions, about 20 percent of its workforce, in the same period it reported record quarterly revenue of $639.8 million, up 34 percent. Its executives said AI use had increased more than 600 percent in three months and that employees were running thousands of AI-agent sessions a day. If AI had been driving the decisions, you would expect the heaviest AI users to be protected, but according to reporting on the earnings call, the company protected salespeople carrying revenue quotas instead, and the cuts reached across every other team and geography.In January 2026 Amazon announced 16,000 corporate job cuts, following 14,000 in October 2025. Washington state filings show the largest category was software development engineers, along with security, data and quality-assurance engineers, applied scientists, UX designers and product managers. Amazon described the cuts as removing layers and bureaucracy. One of those let go was N. Lee Plumb, his team’s head of AI enablement, whom Amazon had flagged as one of the top users of its AI coding tool, Kiro, by his account, only five people in the company used it more. A company replacing people with AI would have little reason to let him go.SAP’s 2024 restructuring affected about 10,000 roles and cost €3.1 billion. Its CFO said the goal was to decouple expenses from revenue growth. The same year SAP created a board-level unit dedicated to moving customers to the cloud. Mainstream support for its ECC system ends in 2027, and SAP has said future innovation, including AI, will be available only in the cloud. Senior executives surveyed by Constellation Research described its RISE migration program as financial engineering more than a benefit to customers.Regulators have documented how hard it is for customers to leave. In November 2024 the US Government Accountability Office found that five of six federal agencies it interviewed had run into restrictive vendor licensing practices. Three were required to buy again licenses they already owned in order to run that software in the cloud. One had to pay to regain ownership of its own data when a contract ended. In July 2025 the UK Competition and Markets Authority concluded that switching between cloud providers was extremely rare and that egress fees and licensing practices were hurting competition. It estimated that prices just 5 percent above competitive levels would cost UK customers about £500 million a year in a market of roughly £10.5 billion.AI gives these companies a forward-looking explanation for cuts that investors reward. The pattern underneath appears more prosaic. Vendors may be cutting the engineers and support staff who understand the customer’s problems. They are putting their headcount and money into the sales teams, migration programs onto platforms with switching costs and contract structures that move customers onto their platforms and keep them there. And they appear to be raising prices on customers whose cost of leaving keeps rising. Customers get less help, pay more and have fewer ways out in this formulation.Enterprise software used to win by building a better product, solving harder problems and giving customers a reason to renew. Today a vendor can do well by building an ecosystem customers can’t easily leave, cutting the cost of serving them and charging the installed base more. Engineering then gets judged by how efficiently the vendor makes money from the customer’s dependence.CIOs and CFOs evaluating a cloud migration or AI rollout may want to look past this year’s budget savings and ask whether the vendor’s product, service and flexibility are improving, or whether their company is just becoming more dependent on a vendor that profits from engineered retention more than satisfaction. A vendor that cuts the engineers who understand its users while protecting the people who lock those users in has stopped competing on product, and its customers usually find that out at renewal.To execute a pivot toward raw infrastructure rent-seeking, corporate leadership almost always chooses a specific archetype of manager we feel, the platform generalist. These leaders’ core competencies are systems integration (without passing the benefit on to customers), horizontal scaling, and cross-application alliances. They don’t see software as a solution that delivers greater benefits to users, they see it as a distribution channel to force consumption of underlying cloud servers.And if some feature or pricing model will lure the unsophisticated into the trap, this manager is willing to be rewarded for it, trading integrity for short-term margin and a hoped-for getaway when the market catches on.Under this framework, specialized, domain-rich product teams are systematically trimmed or ignored to fund massive infrastructure buildouts. This creates an organizational environment of intellectual debt, the company stops asking how to innovate to save its users time, and starts asking what the bare minimum is to prevent a total customer revolt.When a company reaches this stage, it stops creating value and starts extracting rent, it weaponizes its legal departments, licensing audits, and predatory contract bundles to squeeze extra margin out of a captive customer base, and product excellence gives way to operational coercion.The Cost of Losing the Pro-Customer EngineerThe fatal flaw in the rent-seeking playbook is the assumption that your moats are made of stone, when they are actually made of code and human expertise.When an organization defunds its application layer to buy database chips, for instance, it inevitably triggers a catastrophic brain drain. The elite domain specialists, the institutional anchors who spent decades perfecting niche compliance features, complex calculation logic, and granular user workflows, realize there is no longer a seat for them at the table. They leave. Sometimes it’s worse: bad strategy leads companies to escort their best people out the door as they pivot away from the user and toward servicing their debt covenants.Losing a superstar domain specialist is not just an HR headache; it is a structural breach in the corporate moat. Even if the individual is deep inside the org and you think the customers can’t see them, other team members can, and they get the message: caring about the user and customers is not rewarded here, and it’s time to get out while you still can. These specialists you’re losing possess a rare dual capability: they understand the hyper-complex, real-world problems of the industry, and they know exactly where the legacy software’s seams are weak. When an executive lets an elite product leader and engineer walk out the door, they lose their translation shield, and with it the internal credibility required to keep customers from rebelling against an unusable interface.More importantly, they give the open market a weapon. In the modern cloud landscape, enterprise lock-in is ultimately just a data mapping problem. The moment an elite architect leaves and teaches rival platforms or cloud-flexible competitors how to untangle, translate, and automate the migration of your proprietary code, the “divorce-proof” illusion evaporates.The One Ring of the Seven PowersThis is where Hamilton Helmer’s book is instructive. He names switching costs as one of the seven sources of durable competitive advantage, and the most deceptive of them. Switching costs are the one ring that rules them all, they make you feel powerful because people are forced to stay with you, even against their will.But like the ring, the power corrupts the one who wields it. Once you lose your customers’ will, and they must stay with you without choosing you, you have already lost. You are no longer earning loyalty; you are guarding prisoners. And a new wave of enterprises is attacking exactly that vulnerability.The customer’s side of the trap looks a lot like asking the Mafia for a favor. The first offer is generous: a bundled discount, free migration credits, a deal that solves today’s problem. It feels like a friendship. Only later do you learn the favor was never a transaction; it was a debt, and the debt has no payoff date. Every renewal comes with new terms, and every attempt to leave is met with a reminder of what you owe. You didn’t buy a product; you accepted a relationship you can’t exit.The more a business or investor falls into its own trap, using switching costs to save itself and squeeze customers and clients, the more hated it becomes. Even those who stay are like the subjects of a Soviet regime, compliant on the surface, waiting for their chance to escape or overthrow it. When that chance arrives, they take it.This is why switching costs are a toxic, addictive, and self-destructive power to lean into. The more you use it for short-term returns, the more you sacrifice the trust and authenticity on which long-term persistence is best built.The tragedy of the platform generalist is that financial metrics often shield them from reality until it is too late. Because enterprise data gravity is heavy and moving off a core utility layer is a multi-year, multi-million-dollar risk, revenue may continue to climb for years on forced renewals alone.Coming back to VMware under Broadcom returns to a test case. Broadcom’s infrastructure software segment, which includes VMware, reported $6.9 billion in revenue in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, up 19 percent from a year earlier. AT&T alleged in a 2024 lawsuit that Broadcom proposed a 1,050 percent increase to its annual VMware bill. The case was settled out of court.Customers have been slow to leave, however. The CloudBolt survey cited earlier, of 302 IT decision-makers at North American companies with at least 1,000 employees, found that 86 percent were actively reducing their VMware footprint even though only 4% had fully migrated off it. That is the illusion in numbers, revenue climbs on forced renewals while customers plan their exit. CloudBolt sells hybrid cloud management software, so treat its survey as indicative rather than definitive.But a company that takes an anti-customer approach and sells to anti-customer gatekeepers has written its own obituary. It becomes an empire built on quicksand. Modern organizations, the startups, high-growth scale-ups, and developers of the next generation, will avoid these legacy utilities like the plague. They build on open, flexible, product-led architectures designed to remain rent-proof from day one.The lesson for modern tech leaders may be absolute, infrastructure means nothing if the software on top of it is unusable or beige as one revenue leader in professional services and tech said recently.If you strip your company of its product-deep soul to fund a commoditized infrastructure floor, you are not building a permanent monopoly. You are handing agile, user-first challengers a highly profitable opening to deliver a clean-break data blueprint and hollow out your captive customer base from the outside. You might win the budget war today, but you have guaranteed your long-term irrelevance.A simple test, can you say upfront that what you are selling is handcuffs? If, instead, you are selling how cool-looking and comfortable the handcuffs are, you are losing. Your switching costs are someone else’s opportunity, and they are coming for it.Platform lock-in is now big enough to support its own escape industry.Nutanix added 3,000 new customers in fiscal 2026, its third straight year at that pace, and much of that growth came from customers leaving VMware. Red Hat stripped the container features out of OpenShift to give VMware users a product that runs only virtual machines. It says the number of VMs running on that platform grew 417 percent in a year and that its services team has assessed more than 1.46 million VMs for migration. HPE became, in Forrester’s words, the first hardware vendor to build its own virtualization software in response to Broadcom’s takeover of VMware.Many of the people building this escape industry learned the trade inside the platforms customers are now trying to leave. VergeIO, which sells a VMware replacement and recently sped up its migration tools, put former VMware CTO Kit Colbert on its board and hired Parag Patel, a former VMware sales vice president, as CEO. About 19,000 people have left VMware since Broadcom took over. KORE1 says the largest share is landing in the migration practices of system integrators such as Accenture, Deloitte, Kyndryl and HCLTech. A single exit can absorb a team. KORE1 estimates Western Union’s migration of 900 to 1,200 applications needs 30 to 50 engineers. The pattern reaches past VMware. Rimini Street says its primary support engineers average more than 20 years of experience. Dreamteam, founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million for an AI-native CRM and has already replaced Salesforce at DMS Health.At the end of the day, where do you invest into your own tech capabilities, both as an individual advancing your career, or as an enterprise leader or investor? The Jailbreak economy is looking promising.Also, apologies to Thin Lizzy fans for the headline.

item.title: Nvidia Seeded Pirated Books and Shared Them With Adobe, Authors Allege
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: Several book authors have filed (PDF) an amended complaint accusing Nvidia of seeding pirated books via BitTorrent, after downloading them from shadow libraries including Anna's Archive and LibGen. [...] These tools can download files via BitTorrent, and the authors and Nvidia both agree that whether they also upload data to others depends on the settings used. According to the authors, Nvidia didn't prevent seeding altogether. "When Nvidia ran the BitTorrent client, Nvidia uploaded pieces of pirated book files to third parties during the downloading process (i.e., before the download was complete). Nvidia also 'seeded' pirated books (i.e., made available and uploaded parts of a completely downloaded file). While Nvidia took some steps to limit seeding, it did not prevent seeding altogether," the complaint reads.
The authors say they found out in June, when Nvidia handed over the code it used for torrenting. Based on that code, they were "able to determine that Nvidia did not disable uploading," the authors told the court. The complaint states that the authors' own books were among those Nvidia downloaded. However, the claim that they were also uploaded to others is made "on information and belief," which essentially means the authors don't have direct knowledge of it. In addition to the seeding claims, the authors also allege that Nvidia shared the pirated books with business partners, including Adobe, through a "PDF Extraction Project" involving 250 million pages. These pages were acquired in part from shadow libraries such as Anna's Archive and LibGen.
According to the complaint, Nvidia shared its pirated books with Adobe because it wanted to "get tokens out of PDFs to create differentiated models" and "include PDF extraction into our NeMo pipeline so that customers can leverage their PDF content." In return, the complaint says, Adobe committed to using Nvidia's language models in some of its products. That made the deal a big opportunity for Nvidia, with its NeMo AI models potentially "powering every one of Adobe PDFs," the authors write. Adobe wasn't the only partner. The complaint also mentions partnerships with Cohere and Imbue that involved sharing Nvidia's base training data and offering books acquired from shadow libraries. The authors believe their own books were shared with all three companies, but this is alleged on information and belief. With these allegations, the amended complaint now accuses Nvidia of distributing the books itself and of helping others to infringe, which falls under its existing direct and contributory infringement claims.
